subject: Communication
title: Deepfakes: Seeing Isn't Believing
description: A quick win: understand Deepfakes: Seeing Isn't Believing.

hook.text: A video shows a world leader declaring war. It looks real. It sounds real. It's entirely AI-generated.

buildup.text: Deepfakes use AI to create synthetic media — realistic video, audio, and images of real people doing things they never did.

discovery.text: The technology doubles in quality every six months. Detection tools lag behind generation tools in a constant arms race.

twist.text: The biggest threat isn't fake videos. It's the 'liar's dividend' — real evidence dismissed because anything could be fake.

climax.text: In a world where anything can be faked, provenance (verified source) becomes more important than perception.

punchline.text: When seeing isn't believing, trust becomes the rarest currency.

quiz.question: What is the 'liar's dividend' of deepfakes?
options: Real evidence being dismissed as potentially fake

details.summary: Deepfakes use artificial intelligence to create convincingly realistic fake videos, audio, and images. The technology can put words in anyone's mouth and faces on any body. As the technology improves, visual evidence, once the gold standard of proof, becomes unreliable.
details.whyItMatters: Deepfakes threaten the foundation of evidence-based trust. When any video could be fabricated, the very concept of visual proof is undermined.
takeaways: AI can create convincingly realistic fake video and audio
Visual evidence is no longer reliable proof by itself
Detection technology trails behind creation capabilities

faq.question: How can you identify a deepfake?
faq.answer: Look for unnatural blinking, inconsistent lighting, blurred edges around the face, audio that does not match lip movements, and strange artifacts in hair and backgrounds. However, the technology improves rapidly and visual detection is becoming less reliable.

faq.question: What is the biggest threat from deepfake technology?
faq.answer: Beyond individual fakes, the larger threat is the liar's dividend: the ability of anyone to dismiss real evidence as a deepfake. When everything could be fake, nothing can be proven. This meta-effect on trust may be more damaging than any individual deepfake video.
